## Jon Loomer — PHC - Elite doesn't look much like it used to

_From: `[email]` · 2026-06-07T07:15:15+00:00_

96 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Hey, Mark. If you checked out my private membership a few years ago, or if you were a Power Hitters Club - Elite member at some point and moved on, you may not recognize the community it's become. 
 That's fair. It used to be a private group, a weekly webinar, and a steady stream of courses. That was the whole thing, and it was good, but it was mostly me sharing what I knew and you deciding what to do with it. 
 It's a different membership now. 
 The biggest change is that you can review your own account inside Elite. I built four self-audit tools that walk you through the parts of a Meta account where people lose money without realizing it. Two look at your targeting approach. One examines your audience segments. One digs into your conversion reporting, which is where I see the most expensive mistakes. They're in beta, and they already surface things most advertisers never check. 
 Then there's JonBot, which didn't exist in the old version. It can answer your Meta ads questions using everything I've written over the years as its foundation, so you're not waiting on me or digging through old posts to find the one thing you half-remember. 
 I started creating Ad Briefs this year, and it's grown into a full reference library. I update these living documents as Meta changes, which is constantly. 
 And the weekly strategy sessions are still the heart of the community, and that hasn't changed in years. Bringing your actual problem to a group of friendly advertisers who want to help is hard to replace. It's where progress and bonds happen. 
 So if your picture of Elite is a Facebook group and a weekly webinar, that picture is a few years old. Today it's a place to diagnose your account, get your questions answered, and think through your decisions with help. 
 If you want to see what it looks like today, join us here: 
 https://www.jonloomer.com/phc-elite/ 
 As always, I'm here if you have questions. 
 Talk soon, 
 Jon

## Recomendo — How everyday things work / Storied Colors / All Carve Outs

_From: `[email]` · 2026-06-07T09:02:07+00:00_

View this post on the web at https://www.recomendo.com/p/how-everyday-things-work-storied

How everyday things work
Mechanical-pencil.com [ https://substack.com/redirect/b80887ec-529e-43d6-bfe7-ed460bda332a?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] reminds me of the Way Things Work book I loved as a kid, but with 3D animations that make it even more illuminating. Mechanical engineer and artist Bryan Macomber tears down familiar objects — a Pilot G2 retractable pen, a Zippo lighter, a Pez dispenser, a BIC mechanical pencil — and walks you through how each one works, part by part. Watching the push-push mechanism inside a clicky pen click into place is genuinely satisfying. I hope Bryan keeps adding to this series. — MF
Stories about Color
Storied Colors [ https://substack.com/redirect/4a27325d-e9ea-49ea-9f3e-2250aa2c9055?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] is nerdy and delightful. More than 250 colors are indexed and searchable so you can read the stories behind their origin, chemistry and use. This is especially meaningful to me because not only do I pride myself on knowing the various names for different shades of color, but when I was a young weird kid, instead of playing with dolls, I would play with my box of crayons as characters, assigning personalities based on their color. Color has always been a portal to the imaginal for me, rather than just a simple tint. There’s a mention on their website of an upcoming newsletter version that you can sign up for. — CD
Personal recommendations
The hosts of a great podcast we have featured on Recomendo before, Acquired [ https://substack.com/redirect/1bbffd36-2dfb-435e-86a6-ba1a3f179455?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ], conclude each of their 3-hour episodes about legendary companies with several personal recommendations each. These could be any apps, books, destinations, shows, apparel, or devices they have personally enjoyed in the last month. They have good taste, lots of variety and a wide range, over their 10-year run. This sounds familiar! They call these reviews, “carve outs” (not connected to the show’s topic) but they are really Acquired’s version of Recomendo [ https://substack.com/redirect/dc69e952-37fa-4901-80c4-0b125badc7e8?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ]. I’ve found some good stuff this way. — KK
Two smart rings, compared
I’ve been wearing the RingConn Gen 3 [ https://substack.com/redirect/352366a4-0c96-4e95-939d-187569e4b9c1?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] and the Oura Ring 4 [ https://substack.com/redirect/dca4e6a4-a89c-43cf-8008-0fc46a42604b?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] side by side for over a week, and their core tracking is nearly identical — sleep profiles, heart rate, and other vital signs all line up closely between the two. So on accuracy, it’s basically a wash. But I prefer the RingConn for two reasons: it doesn’t charge a $6/month subscription to see your own data, and it lets you export that data — neither of which Oura allows. The RingConn also has vibration alerts for a low battery, too much sitting, and other health nudges (you can silence them while sleeping). The one thing Oura does better: a small dimple that lets you orient the sensors toward your palm. The RingConn lacks that, so it sometimes rotates, and I’m not sure it’s reading accurately. — MF
Meme art
Obsessive effort spent on ridiculous memes, over-the-top projects about stupid things, absurd seriousness about nonsense. Also meticulous craftsmanship at scale: these are the hallmarks of art projects by Sunday Nobody [ https://substack.com/redirect/2babfc1e-1dee-4a6d-87a2-b3c506ee9412?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ], a young “meme artist” who posts on YouTube and Instagram. For a recent example of his gonzo projects, watch his Taco Bell Funeral [ https://substack.com/redirect/ac6cbf5c-2b21-432f-a217-e6f0839beca3?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ]. To finance his performances he sells limited editions of his very collectable art. His real art is the whole nerdy process. — KK
Writer Deck resource list 
Johnny Webber put together a great list of resources [ https://substack.com/redirect/75fef3b5-7cfc-4a45-847d-d4f370024f9b?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] for anyone contemplating purchasing or building their own Writer Deck, a single-purpose, distraction-free writing device. I still use my AlphaSmart Neo2, which I recommended in 2019 [ https://substack.com/redirect/62e43268-bd25-40a7-821a-f52e5503dd7b?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] when you could still find them super cheap on Amazon, and the tactile keyboard feels so satisfying to type on while the battery life lasts for months and months. Someday I might invest in a newly made writer deck, but for now this works. — CD

The New Super IC
****************

So, what is a Super IC?

​Elena describes it ( https://2699bf44.click.kit-mail3.com/38uolwmo80fkh25z4gxbrh4mzgz66crr8z9vdo3gz00qlrxzz98x2l2632q9qp6vekogw2o9xk2w84rw5gg2xk9wv3q7v5kv3p4p5gnvld85gem89e8xelerxkla6788d/48hvh7umeez829uqu7/aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuZWxlbmF2ZXJuYS5jb20vcC9pYy13b3JrLWlzLXRoZS1uZXctY2FyZWVyLWZsZXg= ) as someone who can take a project that delivers real business value and run it end to end, on their own. We're not talking about an early stage employee. It's usually a former manager or director who stepped back into IC work.

To be fair, a similar type of role has existed for some time called the Principal PMM. But it wasn't particularly common. The normal path for most PMMs was to climb the career ladder until you landed a manager-level role. A few landed in a Principal PMM role instead, usually because they had deep subject-matter expertise and a love for the craft. I hired for this role on my teams at Unbounce and Kajabi, and in both cases it focused on the inbound side of PMM.

But that was before AI.

Before, even if you were an experienced IC, taking your strategy from idea to execution meant collaborating with other teams like content, design, and growth. Now, with tools like Claude Code, a PMM can vibe code the landing page, build an interactive demo, create a dashboard, and ship experiments themselves. The work that used to require a team and a few weeks can happen in an afternoon.

Elena makes a great point about why this works. She describes AI as "average intelligence." It won't make you a great designer or a great engineer, but it gets you to average in skills you don't have, and average is often enough to get a real thing into the world.

AI gives everyone the ability to build, regardless of seniority. What it doesn't give them is the judgment to know whether they're solving the right problem. A Super IC pairs the ability to build with the experience to know what's worth building.

This is where the Super IC starts to differ from a traditional Principal PMM. Instead of going deep on one area of expertise, they own something end to end, from inbound to outbound.

In order to succeed in this role, I think you need to combine three sets of skills. Strategy skills help you identify the right opportunity. Maker skills allow you to bring your strategies to life. And credibility skills (think: influence) earn you trust and access to the context you need.

​
What does this mean for people managers?

Elena argues that the management level, especially middle management, is collapsing. Her point is that most of management exists to coordinate work. Managers review work, approve decisions, and move information up and down the business. That made sense when building was slow and expensive, because you needed to get things right before you committed to them.

But when you can build and test something in hours, Elena says it becomes cheaper to just try something rather than to debate it.

That's mostly true, but it creates some downstream implications too.

What happens when you have a company of Super ICs running experiments and shipping rapidly without a manager reviewing the strategy? I think it'll get messy real quick.

Sure, it might be cheaper to build now, but that doesn't mean it comes without a cost. We need to consider the end-customer experience. Customers can only absorb so much information! Think about how overwhelming it would be to be exposed to an influx of experiments, features, and campaigns (especially if some are conflicting).

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Copywriter Eugene Schwartz said something I think about every time I write an ad.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------

“The one thing I hate most in the world and shows me absolute disaster,” he said, “is when somebody comes up to me and says, ‘Wow! That headline is so beautiful. Where did you get those words? They’re gorgeous!’

“I say, Oh no, you’re seeing the words; you’re not seeing through the words. You’re seeing the words themselves. No good.”

----------------------
“Look—” said Schwartz:
----------------------

“If you want to write poetry, if you want to write prose, if you want to write novels, and if you want to write literature, go outside of advertising. Because the words in advertising are like the windows in a store. You must be able to look right through them and see the product. If you see the window, it’s dirty—and you’re going to see yourself or you’re going to see the smear. You’re not going to see the product, and you’re going to lose.”

----------------------------------------------------
Conversion copy should not call attention to itself.
----------------------------------------------------

It should call attention to the prospect, to her problems. Or to the product, to the pleasure it produces or the pain it prevents. But not to itself.

Keep your windows clean.

I chatted with Brandon Metcalf, CEO of Assemble, a company that has 160 human employees and 200 digital workers running alongside them. They've scaled 54x since 2023. Yeah. 54x. I had 1 question for Brandon: How do you actually hire an AI agent the right way? Here's what he told me. 👇 1st, the mindset shift. Stop treating AI like a tool you only use to search things on. Start treating it like a hire you manage. Brandon's words: "What I'm trying to get this AI to deliver is the same thing I look for employees to deliver. There's a job I want done. I know if I coach it, it gets better. If I stop coaching it? It goes sideways." That was the unlock for him. And once you hear it that way, you can't unhear it. Step 1️⃣: Write the actual job description. Before you open ANY platform, open a doc. What is this agent's 1 job? What does it take in? What does it output? What does great look like? What are their KPI's Get that down 1st. Then, you're ready. 🐎 Step 2️⃣: Define what success looks like BEFORE you launch. This is the most skipped step. And it's exactly why AI experiments die quietly after 3 weeks. If YOU don't define what success is, the agent defines it for itself. And that's probably not what you want. Content agent: Define briefs per week, quality bar, format. Email agent: Open rate threshold, sequence length, tone. Get specific. Vague success criteria produce vague agents. Every time. Step 3️⃣: Hire a specialist, not a generalist Brandon learned this the hard way with Bradley, his executive briefing agent. Bradley had too broad a job and kept struggling with sales data. So he built Stanley. 1 job: own the sales pipeline view. That's it. His framework for this is T-shaped leadership. Deep in 1 lane. Aware of the big picture. Same model applies to your agents. One agent for SEO content. One for email nurture. One for paid copy. A focused agent that owns 1 lane will always beat a do-everything agent that owns 12. Step 4️⃣: Coach it every single week. You wouldn't hire someone and ghost them for a month. Same rules apply here. Brandon blocks 20-30 minutes weekly to review output, correct drift, and tighten the brief. He still does it for his agents who report to him, Bradley and Stanley every week. What used to take weeks of back-and-forth now takes an hour and a half. With real-time data he can actually make decisions on. Coaching compounds. Skipping it compounds too. Just not in the good way. Step 5️⃣: Let your humans get promoted. This was the part of the conversation I wasn't expecting. Brandon has an AI SDR named Teddy. Theodore when he's been naughty. 😂 When they were rolling Teddy out, a human SDR named Mitch was put in charge of managing him. Teddy got better. But so did Mitch. Mitch got promoted to AE. First month in the new role? Closed 11 deals. Because managing an AI agent forced him to deeply understand what great outreach actually looks like and he applied it directly to his own work. AI doesn't replace your team. It accelerates the people willing to grow alongside it. The hill Brandon would die on. "You can't slap an agent on anything and think it's going to work. You have to be very clear on what its job is and what makes it successful. Everyone misses that second piece." Tasks without a job. A job without a definition of success. That's where it always breaks down. Define the role. Define what winning looks like. Coach it like a person. The companies doing all 3 right now are pulling away from everyone else. Quietly.
